mainEntity.name: How long does benzodiazepine withdrawal last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Acute withdrawal usually lasts one to four weeks, with the worst symptoms peaking between day 3 and day 10. Short-acting benzodiazepines cause faster, sharper symptoms, while long-acting ones spread out. A minority of people have protracted symptoms that fade over 6 to 18 months.

Yes, it can. Stopping abruptly after long-term use can cause grand mal seizures, dangerously high heart rate and temperature, and delirium. This is why a medically supervised taper is the standard of care and cold turkey is never recommended.

mainEntity.name: What are the first signs of benzo withdrawal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Early signs usually include returning anxiety, restlessness, difficulty sleeping, irritability, and a mild tremor. With short-acting drugs like Xanax these can begin within 6 to 12 hours of the last dose and intensify over the following days if there is no taper.

mainEntity.name: Why can't I just stop taking my benzodiazepine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your brain has adapted to the medication and needs time to readjust. Removing it suddenly leaves the nervous system over-excited, which drives severe anxiety and raises the risk of seizures. A gradual taper lets your brain rebuild its own balance safely.

mainEntity.name: What is the safest way to come off benzodiazepines?

acceptedAnswer.text: The safest way is a slow, doctor-supervised taper, often after switching to a long-acting benzodiazepine like diazepam. Reductions are typically small, around 5 to 10 percent at a time, and get smaller as the dose lowers. This can take weeks to over a year.

mainEntity.name: How long should a benzodiazepine taper take?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no universal answer. Lower-dose, shorter-term users may taper over several weeks, while long-term or high-dose users often need many months or more than a year. The right pace is the one your body tolerates without severe symptoms.

mainEntity.name: What is protracted or post-acute withdrawal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Protracted withdrawal is a set of lingering symptoms, mainly anxiety, insomnia, and cognitive fog, that continue after the acute phase. It affects an estimated 10 to 15 percent of long-term users and usually keeps improving over months, especially with a slow taper.

mainEntity.name: Can I detox from benzodiazepines at home?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only with medical supervision and usually only for lower doses. A doctor can manage a careful outpatient taper at home for some people, but higher doses, long-term use, or any history of seizures generally call for inpatient medical detox.

mainEntity.name: Are Xanax, Ativan, and Klonopin withdrawals different?

acceptedAnswer.text: They follow the same general pattern on different clocks. Xanax and Ativan are shorter-acting, so withdrawal starts sooner and feels sharper. Klonopin is longer-acting, so symptoms arrive later and stretch out. The seizure risk applies to all of them.

mainEntity.name: Does provincial health cover benzodiazepine detox in Canada?

acceptedAnswer.text: Publicly funded detox beds, hospital care, and RAAM clinics are available across Canada, and many withdrawal management services are covered. Private residential programs vary in cost and coverage, so calling a clinic directly is the fastest way to find your options.

mainEntity.name: What medications help with benzodiazepine withdrawal?

acceptedAnswer.text: The main tool is the benzodiazepine taper itself, frequently using long-acting diazepam. Doctors sometimes add other medications to ease specific symptoms such as sleep problems or seizures. There is no single quick-fix drug that replaces a proper taper.

mainEntity.name: Will my anxiety come back worse after stopping?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rebound anxiety during withdrawal often feels worse than the original problem, but it is usually temporary. As the nervous system settles and you build non-drug coping skills through therapy, most people find their baseline anxiety becomes manageable again.

mainEntity.name: Is it safe to mix a taper with other substances?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Combining benzodiazepines with alcohol or opioids is especially dangerous because all three slow breathing, and the mix is a leading factor in overdoses. If other substances are involved, tell your care team so the whole picture can be managed safely at once.

mainEntity.name: How do I help a loved one going through benzo withdrawal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Encourage them to see a doctor or addiction clinic rather than quit cold turkey, and learn the warning signs of a seizure so you can call 911 if needed. Practical support, patience, and helping them get to appointments all make a real difference.

mainEntity.name: Where do I start if I want to quit benzodiazepines in Canada?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with a conversation, either with your family doctor or a walk-in RAAM clinic, and do not adjust your dose until you have a plan. A clinician can set up a taper, arrange detox if needed, and connect you with counselling.

blocks.html: Benzodiazepine Withdrawal: Timeline, Symptoms, and How to Detox Safely in Canada

blocks.text: If a doctor once handed you a small prescription for anxiety or sleep, you never expected to end up here, afraid of what will happen if you stop. Benzodiazepine withdrawal is one of the few kinds of withdrawal that can genuinely be dangerous, and that fact gets lost in a lot of well-meaning advice about just cutting back. For someone who has been taking a benzodiazepine every day for months or years, stopping the wrong way can trigger seizures. It can also drag on far longer than most people are warned about.

Benzodiazepine withdrawal is one of the few kinds of withdrawal that can genuinely be dangerous, and that fact gets lost in a lot of well-meaning advice about just cutting back. For someone who has been taking a benzodiazepine every day for months or years, stopping the wrong way can trigger seizures. It can also drag on far longer than most people are warned about.

blocks.text: This guide walks through what actually happens when the body comes off benzodiazepines: the timeline, the symptoms, why the seizure risk is real, and how a proper taper and medical detox keep you safe. It is written for Canadians, with a close eye on what recovery looks like here in Ontario, and it draws on guidance from sources such as the Canadian Coalition for Seniors’ Mental Health and the British Columbia Centre on Substance Use. If you are in crisis right now, skip ahead and reach out through the drug and alcohol helpline. You do not have to figure this out alone.

blocks.text: What Benzodiazepine Withdrawal Is and Why It Happens
blocks.html: What Benzodiazepine Withdrawal Is and Why It Happens

blocks.text: Benzodiazepines, the group of medications people usually shorten to “benzos,” calm the brain by boosting a chemical messenger called GABA. If you want the full background on the class, we cover what benzodiazepines are in a separate piece. They include familiar names like alprazolam (Xanax), lorazepam (Ativan), clonazepam (Klonopin), and diazepam (Valium). Doctors prescribe them for anxiety, panic attacks, insomnia, seizures, and muscle spasms, and for short bursts they work well.

They include familiar names like alprazolam (Xanax), lorazepam (Ativan), clonazepam (Klonopin), and diazepam (Valium). Doctors prescribe them for anxiety, panic attacks, insomnia, seizures, and muscle spasms, and for short bursts they work well.

blocks.text: The trouble starts when the brain gets used to that extra calming signal. Within a few weeks of daily use it begins to compensate, dialing down its own GABA activity and turning up the excitatory systems to stay balanced. This is physical dependence, and it is not the same thing as being weak or lacking willpower. It is a predictable change in brain chemistry that can happen even when you take the medication exactly as prescribed.

blocks.text: Dependence Versus Addiction
blocks.html: Dependence Versus Addiction

blocks.text: It helps to separate two ideas that often get tangled together. Dependence means your body has adapted and will react if the drug is removed. Addiction, which clinicians now call a substance use disorder, means use has become compulsive and is causing harm even when you want to stop. Plenty of people who take benzodiazepines exactly as directed become dependent without ever developing an addiction. Both situations still need a careful, medically guided withdrawal, because the seizure risk comes from the dependence, not from how the habit started.

blocks.text: Why Stopping Suddenly Is So Risky
blocks.html: Why Stopping Suddenly Is So Risky

blocks.text: When you remove a benzodiazepine quickly, the brain is suddenly left in an over-excited state with nothing to balance it. That rebound is what drives the anxiety, the tremors, and in serious cases the seizures. This is why benzodiazepines sit in the same high-risk category as alcohol when it comes to withdrawal. You can read our companion guide on alcohol withdrawal to see how similar the danger is, since both act on the same GABA system.

blocks.text: The Serious Symptoms That Signal an Emergency
blocks.html: The Serious Symptoms That Signal an Emergency

blocks.text: A smaller set of symptoms means the withdrawal has become dangerous and needs medical attention right away. Seizures are the one everyone worries about, and they can appear in the first few days after an abrupt stop. Other red flags include a dangerously high heart rate, a soaring temperature, hallucinations, severe confusion, and delirium. If any of these show up, call 911 or get to an emergency department. This is not the moment to wait it out at home.

blocks.text: The Benzodiazepine Withdrawal Timeline
blocks.html: The Benzodiazepine Withdrawal Timeline

blocks.text: No two people follow an identical schedule, but the shape of the timeline depends heavily on which benzodiazepine you were taking. Short-acting drugs leave the body fast, so withdrawal starts sooner and hits harder early. Long-acting drugs taper themselves to some degree, so symptoms come on later and spread out.

blocks.text: Short-Acting Versus Long-Acting
blocks.html: Short-Acting Versus Long-Acting

blocks.text: Short-acting benzodiazepines such as alprazolam and lorazepam can produce symptoms within 6 to 12 hours of the last dose, and the acute phase often peaks around days 3 to 7, according to clinical summaries from GoodRx and American Addiction Centers. Long-acting benzodiazepines like diazepam and clonazepam may not trigger noticeable withdrawal for 24 to 48 hours or more, with a later peak around days 5 to 10.

blocks.text: Protracted Withdrawal, the Part Few People Warn You About
blocks.html: Protracted Withdrawal, the Part Few People Warn You About

blocks.text: For roughly 10 to 15 percent of long-term users, symptoms outlast the acute phase and settle into what clinicians call protracted or post-acute withdrawal syndrome. The Benzodiazepine Information Coalition describes waves of anxiety, insomnia, and cognitive difficulty that can continue for months. Most people who taper carefully find these symptoms resolve within 6 to 18 months of the last dose, and a slow, patient taper appears to lower the odds of getting stuck there in the first place.

blocks.text: Why Benzodiazepine Withdrawal Can Be Dangerous
blocks.html: Why Benzodiazepine Withdrawal Can Be Dangerous

blocks.text: It is worth being direct about this, because the stakes are higher than most people assume. Benzodiazepines and alcohol are the two commonly used substances where quitting cold turkey can kill you. Opioid withdrawal is agonizing but rarely fatal on its own. Benzodiazepine withdrawal is the reverse: the symptoms can look milder at first, then turn dangerous quickly.

blocks.text: The Seizure Threat
blocks.html: The Seizure Threat

blocks.text: Grand mal seizures can occur within the first 24 to 72 hours after an abrupt stop, and the risk climbs with higher doses and longer use. A seizure can happen without much warning, and it can cause injury, breathing problems, or worse. This single fact is why every credible guideline says the same thing: do not stop a daily benzodiazepine on your own. A medically supervised medical detox exists precisely to remove this danger.

blocks.text: The Added Danger of Street Benzos in Canada
blocks.html: The Added Danger of Street Benzos in Canada

blocks.text: There is a newer layer to this problem. Benzodiazepines and benzodiazepine-like drugs such as etizolam are increasingly being cut into the illegal opioid supply, a combination sometimes called “benzo dope.” In Ontario, prescription benzodiazepines were detected in roughly 45 percent of opioid toxicity deaths in 2024, up sharply from 33 percent the year before, according to data reported by the CBC. When a benzodiazepine is mixed with fentanyl, naloxone still reverses the opioid, but it does nothing for the benzo, which is one reason overdoses have become harder to treat. If opioids are part of the picture too, our guide to fentanyl addiction in Canada covers that side in detail.

blocks.text: Safe Detox: How a Benzodiazepine Taper Works
blocks.html: Safe Detox: How a Benzodiazepine Taper Works

blocks.text: The single most important idea in benzodiazepine recovery is that you come off slowly, under medical guidance, not all at once. A good taper gives the brain time to rebuild its own GABA balance so the rebound never spikes into something dangerous.

blocks.text: The Long-Acting Substitution Strategy
blocks.html: The Long-Acting Substitution Strategy

blocks.text: A common approach is to switch from a short-acting benzodiazepine to a long-acting one, usually diazepam, before starting the taper. Diazepam has a long half-life and comes in several strengths, which lets a clinician trim the dose in small, even steps and smooth out the peaks and valleys that make short-acting drugs so hard to leave. From there, the dose comes down gradually over weeks or months.

blocks.text: Going Slow and Going Hyperbolic
blocks.html: Going Slow and Going Hyperbolic

blocks.text: Experience and emerging guidance both point the same way: slower is gentler. Many clinicians aim for reductions of around 5 to 10 percent of the dose at a time, with the cuts getting smaller as the dose gets lower. That last part matters. The jump from a small dose to zero is often the hardest, so the taper stretches out near the end rather than finishing abruptly. For some people the whole process takes several months, and for those on high doses it can take a year or more. That is not failure. It is the taper working as designed.

blocks.text: Treatment After Detox: Where Recovery Actually Happens
blocks.html: Treatment After Detox: Where Recovery Actually Happens

blocks.text: Getting through withdrawal is the start, not the finish. Detox clears the drug, but it does nothing about the anxiety, insomnia, or life stress that led to daily use in the first place. The people who stay off benzodiazepines are usually the ones who keep going into real treatment.

blocks.text: Therapy and Skills
blocks.html: Therapy and Skills

blocks.text: Cognitive behavioural therapy has strong evidence for both anxiety and insomnia, which makes it a natural fit for benzodiazepine recovery. Learning to manage panic and sleep without a pill removes the reason the medication felt necessary. Many people benefit from a mix of individual counselling and group work, delivered through structured treatment programs that can run as inpatient or outpatient care depending on your needs.

blocks.text: Treating the Whole Picture
blocks.html: Treating the Whole Picture

blocks.text: Because so many people started benzodiazepines for anxiety, panic, or trauma, treating the underlying mental health condition is part of the work, not a side note. When a substance use problem and a mental health condition sit together, dual diagnosis treatment addresses both at once, which tends to work far better than treating either alone. Planning ahead for triggers through a solid relapse prevention plan gives you something concrete to lean on during the wobbly early months.

blocks.text: Frequently Asked Questions About Benzodiazepine Withdrawal
blocks.html: Frequently Asked Questions About Benzodiazepine Withdrawal

blocks.text: How long does benzodiazepine withdrawal last?
blocks.html: How long does benzodiazepine withdrawal last?

blocks.text: Acute withdrawal usually lasts one to four weeks, with the worst symptoms peaking somewhere between day 3 and day 10. Short-acting benzodiazepines cause faster, sharper symptoms, while long-acting ones spread out. A minority of people have protracted symptoms that fade over 6 to 18 months.

blocks.text: Can benzodiazepine withdrawal kill you?
blocks.html: Can benzodiazepine withdrawal kill you?

blocks.text: Yes, it can, which is what sets it apart from many other withdrawals. Stopping abruptly after long-term use can cause grand mal seizures, dangerously high heart rate and temperature, and delirium. This is why a medically supervised taper is the standard of care and cold turkey is never recommended.

blocks.text: What are the first signs of benzo withdrawal?
blocks.html: What are the first signs of benzo withdrawal?

blocks.text: Early signs usually include returning anxiety, restlessness, difficulty sleeping, irritability, and a mild tremor. With short-acting drugs like Xanax these can begin within 6 to 12 hours of the last dose. They tend to intensify over the following days if there is no taper in place.

blocks.text: Why can’t I just stop taking my benzodiazepine?
blocks.html: Why can’t I just stop taking my benzodiazepine?

blocks.text: Because your brain has adapted to the medication and needs time to readjust. Removing it suddenly leaves the nervous system over-excited, which drives severe anxiety and raises the risk of seizures. A gradual taper lets your brain rebuild its own balance safely.

blocks.text: What is the safest way to come off benzodiazepines?
blocks.html: What is the safest way to come off benzodiazepines?

blocks.text: The safest way is a slow, doctor-supervised taper, often after switching to a long-acting benzodiazepine like diazepam. Reductions are typically small, around 5 to 10 percent at a time, and get smaller as the dose lowers. Depending on the starting dose, this can take weeks to over a year.

Reductions are typically small, around 5 to 10 percent at a time, and get smaller as the dose lowers. Depending on the starting dose, this can take weeks to over a year.

blocks.text: How long should a benzodiazepine taper take?
blocks.html: How long should a benzodiazepine taper take?

blocks.text: There is no universal answer. Lower-dose, shorter-term users may taper over several weeks, while long-term or high-dose users often need many months or more than a year. The right pace is the one your body tolerates without severe symptoms, so tapers are adjusted as you go.

blocks.text: What is protracted or post-acute withdrawal?
blocks.html: What is protracted or post-acute withdrawal?

blocks.text: Protracted withdrawal is a set of lingering symptoms, mainly anxiety, insomnia, and cognitive fog, that continue after the acute phase. It affects an estimated 10 to 15 percent of long-term users. Symptoms come in waves and usually keep improving over months, especially with a slow taper and good support.

blocks.text: Can I detox from benzodiazepines at home?
blocks.html: Can I detox from benzodiazepines at home?

blocks.text: Only with medical supervision and usually only for lower doses. A doctor can manage a careful outpatient taper at home for some people, but this is different from quitting on your own. Higher doses, long-term use, or any history of seizures generally call for inpatient medical detox.

blocks.text: Are Xanax, Ativan, and Klonopin withdrawals different?
blocks.html: Are Xanax, Ativan, and Klonopin withdrawals different?

blocks.text: They follow the same general pattern but on different clocks. Xanax and Ativan are shorter-acting, so withdrawal starts sooner and feels sharper. Klonopin is longer-acting, so symptoms arrive later and stretch out. The underlying seizure risk applies to all of them.

blocks.text: Does insurance or provincial health cover benzodiazepine detox in Canada?
blocks.html: Does insurance or provincial health cover benzodiazepine detox in Canada?

blocks.text: Publicly funded detox beds, hospital care, and RAAM clinics are available across Canada, and many withdrawal management services are covered. Private residential programs vary in cost and coverage. Reviewing how rehab costs and funding work locally, and calling a clinic directly, is the fastest way to find your options.

blocks.text: What medications help with benzodiazepine withdrawal?
blocks.html: What medications help with benzodiazepine withdrawal?

blocks.text: The main tool is the benzodiazepine taper itself, frequently using long-acting diazepam. Doctors sometimes add other medications to ease specific symptoms such as sleep problems or seizures, chosen case by case. There is no single quick-fix drug that replaces a proper taper.

blocks.text: Will my anxiety come back worse after stopping?
blocks.html: Will my anxiety come back worse after stopping?

blocks.text: Rebound anxiety during withdrawal often feels worse than the original problem, which is upsetting but usually temporary. As the nervous system settles and you build non-drug coping skills through therapy, most people find their baseline anxiety becomes manageable, sometimes better than it was on the medication.

blocks.text: Is it safe to mix a taper with other substances?
blocks.html: Is it safe to mix a taper with other substances?

blocks.text: No. Combining benzodiazepines with alcohol or opioids is especially dangerous because all three slow breathing, and the mix is a leading factor in overdoses. If other substances are involved, tell your care team so the whole picture can be managed safely at once.

blocks.text: How do I help a loved one going through benzo withdrawal?
blocks.html: How do I help a loved one going through benzo withdrawal?

blocks.text: Encourage them to see a doctor or addiction clinic rather than quit cold turkey, and learn the warning signs of a seizure so you can call 911 if needed. Practical support, patience during the up-and-down weeks, and helping them get to appointments all make a real difference.

blocks.text: Where do I start if I want to quit benzodiazepines in Canada?
blocks.html: Where do I start if I want to quit benzodiazepines in Canada?

blocks.text: Start with a conversation, either with your family doctor or a walk-in RAAM clinic, and do not adjust your dose until you have a plan. From there a clinician can set up a taper, arrange detox if needed, and connect you with counselling. You can also call a confidential helpline to talk through options first.

blocks.text: A Final Word
blocks.html: A Final Word

blocks.text: Benzodiazepine dependence often begins with a legitimate prescription and a real problem you were trying to solve. There is no shame in where you are, and there is a safe way out. The one thing worth repeating is that this is not a withdrawal to face alone or to rush. With a proper taper, the right medical support, and treatment for what sits underneath, people come off these medications and get their steadiness back every day. If you are ready, a single call to a doctor, a clinic, or a helpline is enough to begin.
